title: How to Match Gold Foil on Perfume Boxes and Paper Bags
seoTitle: Matching Gold Foil on Perfume Boxes & Paper Bags | MTT
summary: Gold foil looks different on a perfume box and paper bag? Compare substrates, foil references and finished samples before approving a coordinated packaging set.
intro: To match gold foil on a perfume box and its paper bag, approve the foil on both actual finished surfaces, side by side. Record the foil reference, paper, coating and finishing sequence for each component. A shared description such as “champagne gold” does not define a reproducible result. Set an agreed appearance reference and inspect complete samples before production, especially when the box uses textured wrapping paper and the bag uses a smooth laminated stock.
cta: Send your box and bag artwork, paper or laminate references, preferred foil sample, quantities and any mismatched samples. MTT can coordinate a finish comparison and sampling brief before you approve the set.
sections: Separate a shade mismatch from a transfer defect

Put the box and bag beside each other under the same light, with their decorated faces at comparable angles. Then rotate them together. Does one gold look consistently warmer, or is one logo simply patchy, dull or missing fine details? Record these as different observations. Changing the gold colour will not necessarily solve incomplete transfer.

A useful approval request names what must match: the gold tone, the reflective character, the sharpness of the logo, or all three. A satin logo and a mirror-bright logo can belong to the same colour family while giving a different visual impression. Decide whether that contrast is intentional before asking a supplier to remove it.
Specify the surface that receives the foil

A rigid box’s greyboard gives the box its structure, but the foil is normally applied to its outer wrapping material or a treated layer above it. For the paper bag, identify the actual printed, coated or laminated face being stamped. “Paper packaging” is too broad a specification for either component.

Holmen Iggesund’s hot foil stamping guidance identifies surface smoothness as important to the appearance of foil and notes that surface irregularities can become more apparent after foiling. That supports checking the real surface rather than judging a foil swatch alone.

For a textured box wrap paired with a smooth bag, we would sample the existing materials first. If the difference is unacceptable, compare a smoother logo area or a different wrap before changing the entire design. Preserve texture where buyers touch the box if that is a deliberate part of the brief.
Keep a separate finish record for each component

• Box: wrap supplier/reference, colour and texture; any print, coating or laminate; foil supplier, shade and application grade; artwork revision and actual logo size.
  • Bag: face paper reference; printing and any laminate or coating; foil reference and grade; actual logo size and position relative to the top fold, gusset and handles.
  • Both: finishing sequence, approved sample identifier, review lighting and the person authorised to approve substitutions.

Colour and application grade should be separate fields. Ask the converter whether the proposed foil grade suits each surface; do not insist on one grade merely because both items are gold. If the two components require different grades, approve their appearance as a pair. A supplier substitution needs a new comparison, not just a note that the colour name stayed the same.
Choose a matching strategy before paying for more samples

Keep both materials: suitable when texture is central to the box design and the bag must retain its chosen surface. Request a paired finish trial and agree how much difference is acceptable. The compromise may be visual coordination rather than identical reflection.

Bring the surfaces closer: consider a smoother wrap or a different bag finish when a closely matched logo is the priority. Check that the material change still works for wrapping, bag folding and the desired feel.

Make the contrast deliberate: use an approved satin-versus-bright direction, or reserve foil for the box and use a coordinated printed mark on the bag. Show the complete set to the decision-maker; an isolated swatch cannot demonstrate whether that design choice works.

KURZ’s matte and pigmented hot-stamping range illustrates that foil decoration includes different surface effects. Product availability does not establish compatibility with a particular MTT specification. Ask for an appropriate trial rather than treating a finish name as an approval.
Use two sample gates: flat decoration, then assembled packaging

First review a stamped trial on the specified box wrap and bag face. Include the actual artwork at final size: a large solid logo and fine lettering should not be represented by the same generic gold square. Ask the converter to check complete coverage, clear counters in small letters and adhesion on that material build. Do not specify universal temperature, pressure or minimum line-width settings from a website; the selected process and artwork need converter review.

Next review the assembled box and bag together. Check whether foil crosses a wrap corner, fold or gusset; whether the image is distorted after assembly; and whether the decorated area rubs against tissue, the box or adjacent bags during normal packing and handling. Agree the handling or rub-check method and acceptance criteria with the supplier. An informal rub check is useful screening, not a claimed standardised durability result.

For the structural review that accompanies finish approval, use the perfume box and matching bag planning guide. A matching decoration does not prove that the finished box fits comfortably inside the bag.
What to do when the samples do not match

• Gold appears different: confirm the foil references, surface specifications and viewing conditions before changing the colour.
  • Coverage looks broken: return an actual sample and mark the affected area. Ask for a material/process trial, rather than approving a retouched photograph.
  • Small lettering fills in: review the final-size artwork with the converter. A revised logo size or spacing may be preferable to repeated trials with unchanged artwork.
  • Flat trials pass but assembled pieces fail: check the decoration position, finishing sequence and handling after stamping. Retain both the flat trial and assembled sample to locate when the problem appears.

Change one main variable per comparison and label every trial. Otherwise a new foil, paper and artwork revision can improve the sample without revealing which change actually solved the problem.
Approve a paired reference, not a screen image

Retain an approved box and bag as the shared physical reference for the buyer and production team. Record the material and artwork revisions, foil details, accepted appearance differences, defect examples and the date of approval. Keep the references protected from damage so a worn sample does not become the next order’s target.

Photos are useful for discussing logo position and obvious defects, but lighting, angle and screen rendering limit colour and reflection comparisons. If approval must happen remotely, send the paired physical samples and agree the review conditions. Do not describe a digital mockup as proof that the gold will match.

For a repeat order, confirm that the wrap, bag surface and foil specification remain available. If any component changes, compare it against the retained set before accepting the replacement. See the packaging sample approval process for the wider sign-off sequence and printing and finishing options for other decoration choices.
